implementerProof.how: Drove the same surface independently on my own database (infra393_test, migrated by the head's binary): the real envoy-dispatch built at 21358491 on Postgres 17.11 + pgvector 0.8.0 in the issue pod, DISPATCH_EMBEDDER=azure keyless (the pod's projected token exchanged at Entra) against the live embed-v-4-0 deployment, with my own content. Settings rows, every boot refusal, the default boot unchanged, the identity filter, coverage without a command, input_type, a 32,000-character body embedded whole, the outage and recovery, and the gcp:Dispatch goldens' environment booting the binary all held, as the proof array below records.

failures.criterion: The server itself embeds everything it holds after boot, including items written before the embedding triggers existed, with no command run by a person (spec line 4; plan Decision 8: the coverage pass at start and every 10 minutes beside the scan loop)
failures.evidence: Run (packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/embedqueue/queue.go:76-80) marks one context with store.WithTransactionTracking and hands it to both runCoverage (its own goroutine) and the scan loop. The pool's hold mark lives in that context (store/pool.go:79-91), so while one loop has a cursor open the other loop's next statement is refused as a nested acquire; store.ForConcurrentRead's doc (pool.go:93-99) names exactly this ('Reads sharing one mark would refuse each other'). Live: booting the head's binary on Azure with 50 pending 32,000-character comments logged 'dispatch: second pooled connection requested while one is held' and 'dispatch embedqueue: coverage pass failed; the next one runs on schedule error="coverage pass: issue: this caller already holds a connection of the pool: a second one would deadlock it"' (stack: Cover coverage.go:217 <- runCoverage <- Run queue.go:78), so the pass that adds pre-trigger items, repairs stale rows and drops foreign vectors stopped and waits 10 minutes; a large production backlog keeps the scan loop's cursors open often, so passes keep failing. The reverse also holds: the pass's Coverage cursor refuses the scan loop's statements, and one loop's release clears the mark the other still needs, so the guard stops protecting either. Red test (commit f2d360158d8bee04cff0a8e158a24c6be6bf6a5e): TestRunsCoveragePassIsNotRefusedWhileTheScanLoopHoldsACursor in packages/envoy/internal/dispatch/embedqueue/coverage_test.go holds the scan loop's claim cursor open through a protocol-pausing proxy while the pass runs. Command: cd packages/envoy && DISPATCH_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres@127.0.0.1:55393/postgres?sslmode=disable go test ./internal/dispatch/embedqueue/ -run TestRunsCoveragePassIsNotRefusedWhileTheScanLoopHoldsACursor -count=1 -v -> FAIL: 'coverage pass failed ... this caller already holds a connection of the pool' then 'after Run: items 3 current 2 lacking 1 failed 0, want all 3 current'. With each loop given its own mark (a throwaway change, reverted: runCoverage on store.ForConcurrentRead(ctx)) the same test passed 3 of 3 runs. No existing test runs Cover beside the scan loop on Run's shared context; the coverage tests call Cover with a context of their own.

risks: A misnamed deployment (or any identity change) drops every vector at the first pass, before a single embedding proves the new place works: live, DISPATCH_AZURE_EMBED_DEPLOYMENT=embed-v-4-0-typo logged foreignVectorsDropped=41 and Azure answered 404 DeploymentNotFound; reverting re-embedded all 42 items. This is plan Decision 8 as approved; the architect decides whether it stays.

azureRequestTimeout (60 s) is shorter than Azure's time for a dense batch: one direct request of 40 CJK bodies (1,049,910 tokens) took 65.0 s and succeeded. Through the server, 50 pending CJK comments timed out once, were bisected and all became current in about 2 minutes, none dead; the timed-out request still spent its tokens.

embed.EstimateTokens (4 characters a token) under-counts dense text: a 32,000-character CJK body is 26,255 tokens and a 32,000-character hex body 28,207, against an estimate of 8,000, so background pacing can exceed the quota and meet Azure's 429, which the queue treats as a throttle.
